books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text:
“I was once a tool of oppression,
And as green as a sucker could be,
And monopolies banded together
To beat a poor hayseed like me.
The railroads and old party bosses
Together did sweetly agree;
And they thought there would be little trouble
In working a hayseed like me.
But now I’ve roused up a little
And their greed and corruption I see,
And the ticket we vote next November
Will be made of hayseeds like me.”

(“The Hayseed,” Farmers’ Alliance song, sung in Kansas in 1890)
stimulus.source_note: “The Hayseed,” Farmers’ Alliance song of the 1890s, sung to the tune of “Save a Poor Sinner Like Me.” Public domain; wording checked against the Nebraska Folklore Pamphlet 18 transcript (Federal Writers’ Project, 1938) of the Farmers’ Alliance paper version.

stem: The singer’s complaint about “monopolies” refers most directly to which of the following?

options.text: Small family farms competing with one another
options.misconception: Small farms are the singers, not the monopolies they complain about.

options.text: Large corporations that controlled railroads and markets
Foreign governments that taxed American goods
options.misconception: No foreign government appears in the song.

options.text: Labor unions that organized factory workers
options.misconception: Unions organized workers; the song blames railroads and bosses, not unions.

rationales.A: The hayseed is the victim in the song, not the monopoly he sings against.
rationales.B: Monopolies banded together, and the railroads worked with party bosses against the farmer.
rationales.C: The song’s enemies are at home: monopolies, railroads, and party bosses.
rationales.D: The song never mentions unions. Its targets are corporations and politicians.
rationales.general:
Turn the song’s names into the thing they name.
1. The singer says monopolies banded together to beat him.
2. He names the railroads and old party bosses as his enemies.
3. Railroads and bosses are large powers that set the farmer’s terms.
4. Large corporations controlling railroads and markets are the monopolies of the song.
Remember: a grievance names its target, and the target names the power.
